extracted.intended_audience: practitioners/trademark attorneys who practice before the USPTO; Office of Enrollment and Discipline and USPTO counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Final Order resolving disciplinary action against a trademark practitioner for permitting impermissible electronic signatures; sets out regulatory obligations, required remedial actions, mitigating/aggravating factors, and agreed sanctions under USPTO rules and TMEP guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic signature requirement (37 C.F.R. § 2.193; TMEP § 611.01(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: The person named as the signatory on an electronic trademark document to be filed with the Office must personally enter his or her electronic signature on the document (i.e., personally enter the combination of letters, numbers, spaces and/or punctuation marks adopted as a signature, placed between two forward slash ("/") symbols in the signature block on the electronic submission).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TMEP guidance: "All documents must be personally signed. ... The person(s) identified as the signatory must manually enter the elements of the electronic signature. Another person (e.g., paralegal, legal assistant, or secretary) may not sign the name of a qualified practitioner or other authorized signatory. ... typing the electronic signature of another person is not a valid signature by that person."

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on others signing in place of the named signatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Another person (including non-practitioner assistants, paralegals, legal assistants, or secretaries) may not sign the name of a qualified practitioner, an authorized signatory, or the client on USPTO trademark electronic submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Just as signing the name of another person on paper does not serve as that person's signature, typing the electronic signature of another person is not a valid signature. Filings (e.g., Statements of Use, declarations) that bear such impermissible signatures are improper and carry statutory warnings about criminal penalties for willful false statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to supervise non-practitioner assistants (37 C.F.R. § 11.503(b); TMEP guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners may delegate tasks to non-practitioner paraprofessionals and other non-practitioner assistants, but where a task is delegated the practitioner must supervise adequately the non-practitioner, including giving appropriate instruction and monitoring the non-practitioner's activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practitioner may be disciplined for failing to take reasonable steps to supervise paraprofessionals—examples include failing to monitor the signature process or otherwise learn whether non-practitioner assistants were actually obtaining the named signatories' signatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent representation requires knowledge of USPTO signature rules (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners have an ethical obligation to provide competent representation, which includes the legal knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation; this reasonably includes being knowledgeable of USPTO regulations and guidance pertaining to electronically signing trademark applications and other trademark documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners representing trademark applicants are reasonably expected to know 37 C.F.R. § 2.193 and the guidance in TMEP § 611.01(c) regarding electronic signatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable diligence and promptness; responsibility over non-practitioners (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.103 and 11.503(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness and bear responsibility for non-practitioners assisting the practitioner; this includes taking reasonable steps before filing to learn whether non-practitioner assistants tasked with obtaining signatures are in fact obtaining them and ensuring filings are signed by the named signatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations include (i) having filings where someone other than the named signatory electronically signed the documents; (ii) not taking reasonable steps to learn whether non-practitioners were impermissibly signing; (iii) not knowing that non-practitioners were signing; and/or (iv) after learning of the practice, not promptly notifying clients or the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication obligations to clients (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a),(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: After learning of impermissible signature practices, practitioners must promptly inform clients about impermissibly signed filings and the status of their pending applications/registrations, reasonably explain potential adverse consequences, and consult with clients so they can make informed decisions regarding representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners are expected to reasonably consult with clients about who is authorized to sign, keep clients informed about who signed documents, explain whether electronic signing by others may jeopardize intellectual property rights, and consult about limitations on the practitioner's conduct if a client expects assistance not permitted by the Rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor to the tribunal and remedial measures (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1),(a)(3),(b),(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not make false statements of fact or law to a tribunal or fail to correct a false statement of material fact or law previously made; if a practitioner learns material evidence is false, the practitioner shall take reasonable remedial measures, including, if necessary, disclosure to the USPTO; practitioners must disclose fraudulent conduct related to examination and take remedial measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If compliance requires disclosure of information otherwise protected, the practitioner may still be required to disclose (see 37 C.F.R. § 11.106 and § 11.303(d)). Reasonable remedial measures include informing the USPTO that the named signatory did not sign the document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on misrepresentation and conduct prejudicial to USPTO (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c),(d),(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not file or allow to be filed trademark filings (including declarations) that are not signed by the named signatory; filing or permitting such documents constitutes misrepresentation or conduct prejudicial to the USPTO and may reflect adversely on fitness to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trademark filings bearing impermissible declarations are relied upon by the USPTO when examining, registering, and renewing marks; if signed by an unauthorized signatory, a resulting registration may be invalid and the integrity of the federal trademark registration process is harmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to promptly correct or notify upon discovering impermissible signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: After learning that filings were impermissibly signed, practitioners are required to promptly notify affected clients and the USPTO and to take reasonable remedial measures regarding the filings and declarations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific remedial measures include notifying clients about the implications, informing the USPTO that the named signatory did not sign, and taking steps to identify affected applications and registrations so clients can make informed decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for failure to comply and disciplinary procedures (sanctions and show-cause process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions used in this matter include a public reprimand and one-year probation; during probation the practitioner may continue to practice in trademark and other non-patent matters unless probation is revoked and suspension ordered. The OED Director may issue an Order to Show Cause and seek immediate suspension for up to twelve months if the practitioner fails to comply with USPTO Rules during probation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural steps: OED issues Order to Show Cause, sends to last address of record, grants 15 days to respond; after consideration, OED may deliver the Order, responses, and supporting evidence to the USPTO Director and request immediate suspension; the OED Director will publish the Final Order in the OED FOIA Reading Room and cause publication in the Official Gazette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating and aggravating factors considered in discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors considered include absence of prior public discipline, acknowledgment of ethical lapses, genuine contrition, acceptance of responsibility, cooperation with OED's investigation, corrective actions taken (retraining, development of internal audit team), and any delay or failures in notifying clients or the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order notes that cooperation and corrective steps (e.g., retraining, internal audit team) were mitigating; conversely, the existence of the impermissible practice prior to the practitioner's tenure and delay in notifying clients/USPTO are relevant considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of impermissible signatures on trademark rights and registration validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Impermissibly signed trademark filings—especially declarations—may jeopardize the validity of the application, registration, or renewal; such filings can adversely affect clients' intellectual property rights and the integrity of the trademark registration process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order explicitly warns that willful false statements are punishable under 18 U.S.C. § 1001 and that if a filing is signed by an unauthorized signatory a resulting registration may be invalid. Practitioners must consider these risks when evaluating filings and advising clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement terms: waivers and allocation of costs
rubrics_metrics.description: As part of the settlement, the respondent waived rights to seek reconsideration or review under 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.56 and 11.57 and to otherwise appeal; each party bears its own costs incurred to date and in carrying out the Agreement and any Final Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are procedural terms of the agreed disposition and may be expected in settlement agreements resolving disciplinary matters with the OED.
